clue.text: Ashes to Ashes plot overlooked by 7?

definitions.text: Ashes to Ashes plot overlooked by 7?

parts.words: Ashes to Ashes plot overlooked by 7?
parts.note: 'ashes to ashes' is from the burial service, so the plot is a grave site, and 7 is the house where the parish priest lives next to the church

explanation.surface: Sounds like a remark about the storyline of the TV drama Ashes to Ashes being missed by someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ashes to Ashes' looks like the BBC police drama, and 'plot' like its storyline; here they mean a burial plot. The answer to 7 is the house where a vicar lives.
explanation.definitionFit: A burial ground beside a church is where graves lie within sight of the parish priest's house.

clue.text: As some Europeans withdraw advertisement, Grauniad goes bust

definitions.note: a group of peoples of eastern Europe and western Siberia, such as Hungarians

indicators.note: going bust means breaking apart, so the remaining letters are rearranged
to withdraw something is to pull it out, so these letters are removed from the newspaper's nickname

parts.note: an advertisement is an ad

explanation.surface: A newspaper story: the Guardian, nicknamed the Grauniad, loses its advertisers and folds.
explanation.walkthrough: The Grauniad is the long-standing joke name for the Guardian newspaper, famous for its misprints. 'goes bust' rearranges GRAUNI, what is left once 'withdraw' removes AD.
explanation.definitionFit: Ugrians are the Hungarian-related peoples of the Finno-Ugric language family, partly living in Europe.

clue.text: Macbeth cast, clutching Oscar: "it was quite a sacrifice"

indicators.note: clutching means holding tight inside, so one piece goes within the other
as in casting metal or casting dice, the word Macbeth is thrown into a new shape

parts.note: Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A theatre company picks up an Academy Award for Macbeth, which cost them a great deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cast' looks like the actors in the play, but it rearranges MACBETH, and 'clutching' puts O inside.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Greece a hecatomb was a great public offering of a hundred oxen, so a very large sacrifice.

clue.text: Goddess glimpsed in the raw

indicators.note: glimpsed in says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A goddess is caught sight of naked, as in many a myth.
explanation.definitionFit: Queen of the Olympian deities in Greek myth, wife of Zeus.

clue.text: Tumultuous, sturdy support for Chuck Yeager's debut

indicators.note: in a down entry the supporting piece sits underneath, so it comes after the pieces above it

parts.note: to chuck is to throw, or hurl

indicators.note: a debut is a first appearance, so only the opening letter of the name is used

parts.note: sturdy means burly, strongly built

explanation.surface: A rough ride, with a stout support for the first flight of the famous test pilot Chuck Yeager.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chuck' looks like part of the pilot's name but is a verb meaning throw. Chuck Yeager was the American pilot who first broke the sound barrier.
explanation.definitionFit: A hurly-burly is a noisy commotion, and the word is also used as an adjective for something chaotic and turbulent.

clue.text: RBS misery allegedly finished off old Scottish general

definitions.note: a general who was killed off: a past-participle phrase used as a description

indicators.note: allegedly suggests something is only said to be so, signalling a word that merely sounds like another

parts.note: RBS, the Royal Bank of Scotland, is a bank, and misery is woe

explanation.surface: Reads like a headline: the Royal Bank of Scotland's troubles are said to have done for an old military man.
explanation.walkthrough: RBS is the Royal Bank of Scotland, which needed a government bailout in 2008. 'Bank woe' said aloud gives the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Banquo is the Scottish general in Shakespeare's Macbeth who is murdered on Macbeth's orders.

clue.text: Served up some vinegar? A civilised house!

indicators.note: Served up says the hidden letters are read backwards
some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A diner is offered vinegar and finds it a very refined establishment.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'up' means read from bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: A vicarage is the residence provided for a parish priest, so a specific kind of house.

clue.text: On a poetic evening, knight rolled a joint

indicators.note: rolled means turned over, so the letters run in the opposite direction

parts.note: e'en is a poetic contraction of evening
K is the abbreviation for a knight, as in KBE

explanation.surface: One poetic evening a knight rolled a cannabis cigarette.
explanation.walkthrough: 'joint' looks like a rolled cigarette, which 'rolled' supports; it is a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: The knee is the hinge joint between thigh and lower leg.

clue.text: Open University hired teaching labour to provide this

definitions.text: Open University hired teaching labour to provide this

indicators.note: to labour is to work hard, so these letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: OU is the Open University, the UK's distance-learning university

explanation.surface: The Open University took on staff to deliver what it offers students.
explanation.walkthrough: 'labour' looks like the workforce hired, but it rearranges OU, HIRED and TEACHING. The whole clue also describes what a university provides.
explanation.definitionFit: Universities exist to offer study beyond school level, which is what the Open University hires tutors for.

clue.text: Indian side rejecting a pitch hosting international

indicators.note: hosting means having a guest inside, so one piece goes within the other
rejecting means turning back, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: pitch is the black tarry substance, tar

explanation.surface: A cricket team from India refuses to play on a ground that is staging a Test match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indian side' and 'pitch' suggest cricket, but the side is a side dish. 'rejecting' turns A TAR into RATA.
explanation.definitionFit: Raita is a yoghurt dish served alongside curries in Indian cooking.

clue.text: Going round playing Even Stevens

definitions.meaning: in golf match play, the state of a match level partway through a round
a colloquial phrase for being level or quits

explanation.surface: Two golfers out on the course are neck and neck.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses describe a contest in which neither side leads, the golf term and the general colloquialism for being level.

clue.text: Outstripping ET, Macbeth's on a roll; it's just below Taxi Driver

indicators.note: to roll is to tumble over and over, so the remaining letters are mixed up
outstripping is read as stripping out, so these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A film-chart report: Macbeth is doing well, passing ET and sitting just behind Taxi Driver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on a roll' looks like one phrase; 'on a' is fodder and 'roll' rearranges MACBHSONA, left once ET is stripped out. Taxi Driver looks like the Scorsese film; in a hansom cab the driver sits high at the back, above the cab.
explanation.definitionFit: A hansom is a two-wheeled horse-drawn cab for hire whose driver sits on a raised seat behind and above it.

clue.text: Angry workers hold Julius hostage; they're quite flaky

indicators.note: hold means keep inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: angry means cross
Julius is the setter, who refers to himself, so the letter I
ants are the classic crossword workers, from worker ants

explanation.surface: Furious strikers take the setter hostage, and they are not very reliable.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter calling himself by his pseudonym gives I, the first person. 'flaky' looks like unreliable; it means made of flakes of pastry.
explanation.definitionFit: These French breakfast pastries are made from laminated dough that flakes when bitten.

clue.text: Flaubert's Emma goes topless for female part

indicators.note: going topless means losing the top, so the first letter is removed

parts.note: Emma Bovary is the heroine of Flaubert's novel Madame Bovary

explanation.surface: A literary heroine strips off for a racy role as a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'female part' suggests an acting role, but it is part of the female body.
explanation.definitionFit: The ovary is the female reproductive organ that produces eggs.

clue.text: The old way The Queen's received Sir Robin in the recent past

parts.note: ye is an old way of writing 'the', as in Ye Olde Tea Shoppe
ST, short for street, is a way

indicators.note: received means taken in, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: ER is the Queen (Elizabeth Regina), and the 's adds S
Sir Robin Day was a famous British political broadcaster

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned account of the monarch receiving a knight not long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Robin Day was a famously combative BBC interviewer, knighted in 1981.
explanation.definitionFit: The plural noun means times gone by, especially not long gone, as in the song about all my troubles.

clue.text: If they're being honest, they've never seen a ghost in their lives

definitions.text: If they're being honest, they've never seen a ghost in their lives

parts.words: If they're being honest, they've never seen a ghost in their lives
parts.note: a ghost is a ghostwriter, and 'their lives' are the books they write about themselves; honest ones wrote their own

explanation.surface: Sceptics who admit they have never had a supernatural experience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ghost' looks like a spirit; it means a ghostwriter, who secretly writes books published under someone else's name.
explanation.definitionFit: People who write their own life stories need no hired writer if they did the work themselves.

clue.text: Exam passed quickly (as did Chuck Yeager)

parts.note: an exam is a test
time that passed quickly flew

explanation.surface: A student sails through an exam, just as the famous pilot zoomed through the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: Chuck Yeager was an American test pilot, the first to fly faster than sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeager's career was trialling new aircraft, flying them to check their performance.

clue.text: In Bonn, I get taken in by fake diamond; it's an imitation

indicators.note: taken in by means enclosed by, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: paste is a glass used to make imitation gems
the German for I is ich, Bonn being a German city

explanation.surface: A German is fooled by a false jewel, a mere copy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken in' looks like 'fooled', but here it is literal: put inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastiche is a work that copies the style of another artist or period.

clue.text: Scot assumes Scotland's crown, lifeless

indicators.note: to assume is to take on, so one piece takes another inside

parts.note: scot is an old word for a tax or levy (as in scot-free), so a duty

indicators.note: the crown of something is its top, so only the first letter is used

explanation.surface: A Scotsman takes the throne of Scotland but shows no spark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scot' looks like a Scotsman, but it is the old word for a tax, surviving in 'scot-free'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dry and dull, without animation, can be described as dry as dust.

clue.text: Jester informally greeting Little Richard

parts.note: yo is a casual hello
Rick is a short form of the name Richard

explanation.surface: A clown casually says hello to the rock and roll star Little Richard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little Richard' looks like the singer; it means a short form of Richard.
explanation.definitionFit: Yorick is the dead court jester whose skull Hamlet holds.

clue.text: Twain's hero's 'unter reportedly served in Asian restaurant

definitions.note: describes something brought to the table at an Asian meal

indicators.note: reportedly means as people say it, so the words are taken by their sound

parts.note: Mark Twain's hero is Tom Sawyer; a hunter is a horse, and dropping the h as the apostrophe shows gives 'orse

explanation.surface: Tom Sawyer's horse is supposedly on the menu at an Asian eatery.
explanation.walkthrough: A hunter is a horse ridden to hounds; ''unter' signals the dropped h of Cockney speech, so 'Sawyer's 'orse' said aloud gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The salty fermented-bean condiment is a staple on Chinese and Japanese tables.

clue.text: Open champion from Jamaica knocks out South Africa and Italy

indicators.note: knocking out means removing, so these letters are taken away

parts.note: Usain Bolt is the Jamaican Olympic sprint champion
I is the international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: A Jamaican athlete beats rivals from South Africa and Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Open' looks like a championship event; here it is a verb, to unlock.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw back the bolt of a door is to unfasten it.

clue.text: I wore my mink at dinner to provoke anger

parts.note: wearing a mink coat is being in fur
having been at dinner, I ate

explanation.surface: A diner wears a fur coat to a meal, deliberately upsetting animal-rights campaigners.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue says 'I, in fur, ate': the pieces are read in a different order from the words.
explanation.definitionFit: To make someone furious is to enrage them, stirring their temper.

clue.text: Enthusiastic about International Open

parts.note: O, an unclosed ring, stands for open, as on taps and switch markings

explanation.surface: Someone keen on a golf or tennis tournament called the International Open.
explanation.definitionFit: Being keen on something is an informal sense: someone who loves jazz is really into it.

clue.text: The death of old technology?

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
IT is information technology

explanation.surface: Asks whether something marks the end of outdated machinery.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor's departure from the stage is the old figurative sense for a person's departure from life.

clue.text: Put in position, I have a qualification to work in 9

parts.note: 'I have a BEd' is the same claim as 'I'm a BEd', so I have becomes I'm
BEd, Bachelor of Education, is a degree in the field of the across clue, a teaching qualification

explanation.surface: A job applicant states they hold a degree to teach at university.
explanation.walkthrough: 9 is HIGHER EDUCATION; a BEd is a Bachelor of Education degree. 'Imbed' is a variant of embed.
explanation.definitionFit: To embed or imbed something is to fix it firmly in place within a surrounding mass.

clue.text: Heads of Tottenham Hotspur and Everton join City to splash out for second title

indicators.note: the heads of the words are their opening letters
out means wrong or disordered, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Football news: Spurs and Everton bosses team up with Manchester City to spend big on a second trophy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'splash out' looks like the indicator, but SPLASH is fodder: 'out' alone rearranges CITY TO SPLASH. Actors avoid saying 'Macbeth' in a theatre, so the play has this second name.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatrical superstition gives Shakespeare's Macbeth an alternative name so actors avoid the unlucky word.
